Second, it must be ‘evident’ that the promisor will not perform their obliga­
tion by the due date. Mere suspicion or risk of breach will not do. This protects the 
promisor, who after all has not actually committed a breach and for whom being 
deprived of the promised counter-​performance may have significant negative 
consequences.21
Third, formal notice of the suspension of performance must be given to the 
promisor ‘as soon as possible’. There is, however, no need for the notice to set out 
the grounds that are relied upon, which is required for self-​help termination22 and 
would have been more protective of the promisor.23 He would have had a written 
statement of the reasoning of the promisee and thereby been better placed to chal­
lenge the suspension or alternatively assuage the concerns that prompted it.24
B  Enforced Performance in Kind
In sub-​section 2 of the new Civil Code under the heading ‘Enforced Performance 
In Kind’ are set out the remedies that compel the defaulting party either person­
ally to perform their contractual obligations (referred to herein as ‘specific en­
forcement’) or to pay a third party to do so in replacement or substitution of the 
promised performance (referred to as ‘replacement’).
1  Specific enforcement: compelling the defaulting party 
to perform (exécution forcée en nature)
Civil Code
Art. 1124.—​A unilateral promise is a contract by which one party, the promisor, 
grants another, the beneficiary, a right to have the option to conclude a contract 
whose essential elements are determined, and for the formation of which only 
the consent of the beneficiary is missing.
Revocation of the promise during the period allowed to the beneficiary to ex­
ercise the option does not prevent the formation of the contract which was 
promised.
A contract concluded in breach of a unilateral promise with a third party who 
knew of its existence, is a nullity.
